summary: A tribute to Jon, delivered at UCLA on October 30, 1998, in memory of Jon Postel by his longtime colleague Danny Cohen. It recalls their years working together on Internet projects at ISI. It is a personal memorial, not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a speech about a good friend and coworker who had died, remembering what it was like to work with him every day.

subtitle: A personal tribute to Jon Postel, the Internet's custodian and visionary editor.

tldr.problem: Jon Postel, a foundational figure in the Internet who guided standards, shaped the RFC process, and served as IANA director, passed away unexpectedly.
tldr.mechanism: Danny Cohen, who worked alongside Postel at the Information Sciences Institute for 16 years, delivered a tribute at UCLA recounting their collaboration and Postel's impact on Internet standards and culture.
tldr.outcome: The tribute captures how Postel's dedication, judgment, and insistence on quality—not politics—enabled the Internet to prevail over competing proposals and become the open, decentralized system it is.

today: RFC 2441 is a historical memorial to Jon Postel, published shortly after his death. It stands as a personal record of his impact on Internet development and the deep respect he earned from his colleagues through decades of dedicated, humble work on behalf of the Internet community.

sections.title: A Partnership in Internet Work
sections.content:
RFC 2441 is not a technical specification, but a personal tribute to Jon Postel delivered by Danny Cohen at UCLA on October 30, 1998. Cohen and Postel worked together at the Information Sciences Institute (ISI) for 16 years, from 1977 to 1993, on fundamental Internet projects.

Cohen describes their relationship as a true collaboration, not a hierarchy. They shared offices, worked on the same problems, and supported each other's efforts to advance Internet technology, even when they pursued different projects. Their work together left a lasting mark on Internet standards and protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a speech about a friend who was very important to the Internet. The friend and the speaker worked together for 16 years at a research center, always helping each other.

sections.title: Technical Collaboration and Innovation
sections.content:
Cohen recalls specific projects undertaken with Postel. In 1973, Cohen had done interactive flight simulation over the ARPAnet and brought that experience to ISI. He then worked on interactive speech over the ARPAnet, which led to the formation of the Network Working Group and the "Internet Concepts" project.

One memorable collaboration was solving email interoperability in 1980 during the MOSIS project. When commercial mail systems refused to interoperate, Cohen and Postel spent a long night of hacking that created the mail-tunnel technology behind "InterMail," enabling email exchange between incompatible systems like MCImail and IEEE's COMPmail.

Cohen emphasizes that they worked on these projects not because they were assigned to, but because the problems were worth solving and interoperability was their shared conviction.
sections.plainLanguage: They worked on hard problems together, like making email systems talk to each other. They did this work because they believed it was the right thing to do, even when they were not supposed to.

sections.title: Postel's Role in Standards and the RFC Process
sections.content:
Cohen emphasizes that Postel did not merely edit RFCs for grammar or format. As the corporate memory of the Internet, Postel repeatedly directed RFC authors to earlier related work, helping them improve their specifications by building on what had come before.

Postel served as the IANA director and set the standards for Internet standardization itself. He transformed RFCs from informal documents into the central mechanism for developing Internet standards. Cohen credits Postel's vision and quality standards—not bureaucracy or politics—with enabling the Internet to succeed where other competing technologies like OSI and GOSIP failed.

Postel believed in substance over form. He resisted fancy formatting and insisted on plain ASCII RFCs that could be emailed and read anywhere in the world. For him, content and interesting ideas mattered far more than visual presentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Jon was in charge of the rule book for the Internet. He made sure the rules were good by telling people to learn from older rules. He said the rules should be simple and clear, not fancy. He cared about good ideas, not pretty pictures.

sections.title: Authority Without Bureaucracy
sections.content:
Cohen describes Postel as an authority without bureaucracy. Postel's authority did not come from a management structure or title. It stemmed from his personality, his deep understanding of Internet technology, his unwavering dedication, and his demanding technical taste and style.

This was essential during the 1980s and 1990s when the Internet faced competition from government-mandated standards like OSI and the US government's GOSIP (Government Open Systems Interconnection Profile). While those efforts emphasized prestige and mandates, the Internet community—guided by Postel's judgment and quality standards—had working systems and properly documented protocols.

Cohen notes that Los-Nettos, a regional network initiative, succeeded without lawyers or formal contracts—just handshakes. Postel was interested only in solving the problem, not in expansion, glory, or fortune.
sections.plainLanguage: Jon was a leader, but not because he had a fancy title or rules to follow. People listened to him because he was smart, cared deeply, and always made good choices. He did not like unnecessary rules or fancy meetings.

sections.title: Character and Legacy
sections.content:
Cohen remembers Postel as pleasant, funny, and unselfish. He was full of humor, mischief, and a spirit of adventure. Postel cared deeply about the people he worked with and about the projects they undertook.

The Internet was not a job for Postel but a hobby and a mission in life. He served as the corporate memory, the corporate style, and the corporate taste of the Internet itself. When fancy formatting began to creep into the Internet community, Postel resisted it, insisting instead on simplicity and substance.

Cohen ends the tribute with a simple summary: Postel was an Internet missionary. He was a great friend who is deeply missed. He set the standards not just for Internet protocols but for the entire standardization process and for how the Internet community conducts itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Jon was kind, funny, and cared about people. He loved the Internet so much that it was his life's mission. He believed in doing good work and being honest. People will always remember him.
